newsitem.title: GERMANY: German state says racist motive for blaze unlikely.
newsitem.headline: German state says racist motive for blaze unlikely.

text.p: A senior official in the German state where three Turks died after an arson attack on their apartment said on Thursday there was probably no racist motive behind the blaze.

North Rhine-Westphalia Interior Minister Franz Josef Kniola said a racist motive could "almost be ruled out" because combustible materials which started the fire were found mostly inside the apartment and only a few in the hallway outside.

Kniola said the door of the apartment was closed when fire-fighters arrived and these facts meant the case did not look like a racist attack. He said police were following a series of clues that could not be made public yet.

Three members of a Turkish family died after the blaze broke out in their apartment in the western town of Krefeld on Monday. One man died in the blaze and two women died from injuries they sustained jumping from the third-floor flat.
A leader of Germany's Turkish community called on the country to do more to protect foreigners, although he admitted it was not yet clear if racism was behind the arson attack.

"It is not as if racism does not exist in Germany," Arif Ordu, a senior member of the Council of Turkish citizens in Germany, told Saar Radio. He said Bonn should do more to integrate Turks into German society.

Germany on Wednesday rejected criticism by Turkey's Islamist prime minister, Necmettin Erbakan, over the deaths of Turks in a recent spate of fires in Europe, which he said were the result of rising anti-Moslem sentiment in the West.
A Turkish man was injured on Tuesday after a fire broke out at his home in the western German town of Haigerseelbach. Police found a Nazi swastika symbol spray-painted on the building.
Six Turks died in a fire in the Netherlands last week and Turkish State Minister Lutfu Esengun travelled there on Wednesday to monitor police investigations into the attack.
But German press commentators said Turkey had over-reacted to the fires.

"What we have heard from the Turkish Prime Minister Erkaban and now also the Foreign Ministry has little to do with diplomacy and something to do with propaganda," the daily newspaper Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung said.

The daily Die Welt called coverage of the fires in the Turkish press "hysterical". "Cases which have already been solved show many similar attacks were the result of personal or business feuds between Turks or between Turks and Kurds," it wrote.
Germany suffered a wave of racist violence following unification in 1990, particularly in the formerly communist east. Some commentators fear economic problems are leading to a new surge of racism.
